summary: The reader is built to feel nostalgia, jealousy, and the sadness of time from inside, to labor through the sentences, and to share the joy of memory recovered.

need-to-breathe.why: The narrator's asthma is told, not built to make the reader short of breath; the long sentences come closer.

hungry.why: Françoise's boeuf mode and the asparagus are described so lovingly that a reader's appetite may stir.

full.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

thirsty.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

gassy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-poop.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-pee.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

sleepy.why: The opening pages on falling asleep and waking are built to induce their own drowsy half-state in the reader.

nauseous.why: Nothing is built to sicken the reader.

urge-to-sneeze.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

urge-to-cough.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

dizzy.why: Nothing is built to produce vertigo.

fatigued.why: The reader's fatigue is mental, not bodily.

pain.why: The grandmother's death agony is told with enough precision to make the reader wince.

disgusted.why: Mlle Vinteuil's profanation of her father's photograph and Charlus chained in Jupien's brothel are built to produce revulsion.

itchy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

tickled.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

over-stimulated.why: Nothing is built to overwhelm the senses.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Nothing is built to make the reader feel heat or cold.

afraid.why: The bombardment of Paris and Charlus's night walks give a faint fear; the novel does not aim to frighten.

anxious.why: The child's wait for the goodnight kiss and the narrator's interrogations of Albertine are built to make the reader share the anguish.

panic.why: Albertine's departure is built as a shock the reader feels with the narrator, briefly.

sensory-pleasures.why: The madeleine, the hawthorns, the asparagus, and the smell of Combray's rooms are built to give the reader the senses' pleasures secondhand.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The sentences themselves, the Vinteuil sonata, Elstir's paintings, and the patch of yellow wall are built as aesthetic experience for the reader.

piquancy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

fun-excitement.why: The games with Gilberte and the little band give slight excitement; the novel is not built for thrills.

orgasm.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

love-romantic.why: Swann's and the narrator's loves are rendered from inside so the reader feels their pull, and then their emptiness.

love-family.why: The mother's kiss and the grandmother's devotion are built to touch the reader's own family feeling.

grief.why: The grandmother's death and its delayed grief at Balbec are built to make the reader grieve with the narrator, a year late.

missing-someone.why: The longing for the mother, for Odette, for Albertine is the reader's by immersion.

aroused-sexually.why: Charlus and Jupien's courtship and the narrator's desire are observed rather than built to arouse.

liking-as-a-friend.why: The reader is built to like the grandmother, Saint-Loup, and Françoise, and to warm even to Charlus.

empathy.why: The first-person analysis of every motive makes the reader feel Swann's jealousy, the narrator's anguish, and the snobs' snobbery from within.

compassion.why: The grandmother's death, Charlus's degradation, and Swann's wasted love are built to produce pity.

grateful.why: Nothing is built to make the reader grateful.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

trustful-distrustful.why: The reader is made to weigh Odette's and Albertine's words with Swann and the narrator, never sure of the truth.

depressed.why: The narrator's long inertia can weigh on the reader, though the novel aims at melancholy, not despair.

angry.why: Charlus's rages and Mme Verdurin's cruelty may anger a reader, mildly.

envious.why: Nothing is built to produce envy.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Swann in Love and The Captive are anatomies of jealousy built to make the reader feel its logic from inside.

jealous-friendship.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

hatred.why: No one is built to be hated; even Mme Verdurin is comic.

contempt.why: Legrandin's snobbery, Bloch's gaffes, and the Verdurins' affectations are built for the reader's scorn.

resentment.why: The reader feels the injustice of the Dreyfus affair's social cruelty and of Charlus's humiliation.

proud.why: Nothing is built to make the reader proud.

amused.why: Dr Cottard's puns, Mme Verdurin's swoons, Françoise's malapropisms, and the satire of the salons are built for laughter.

sense-of-belonging.why: The reader is admitted to the salons without being recruited to them.

lonely.why: The narrator's years of illness and solitude are built to make the reader feel isolation.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The Dreyfus affair, Mlle Vinteuil's sadism, and the cruelty of the salons are built to engage the reader's judgment.

admiration.why: The reader is built to admire Bergotte, Elstir, Vinteuil, and the grandmother, and the author's own achievement.

embarrassed.why: Bloch's gaffes, Legrandin caught snubbing, and the narrator's blunders are built for secondhand embarrassment.

shame.why: The reader feels Swann's shame at his wasted love from within but is not shamed.

guilt.why: The narrator's remorse over his grandmother may touch a reader's own.

sad.why: The sadness of time passing is the effect the whole novel is built to produce.

happy.why: Combray's summers are built to give the reader a happiness designed to be lost.

joyful-euphoric.why: The madeleine and the paving stones are built to give the reader the narrator's joy of recovered time.

effort.why: Three thousand pages of long sentences and slow time make the reader's persistence a theme in itself.

focused-in-flow.why: Swann in Love and the Guermantes dinners can absorb a reader, but the novel's pace resists flow by design.

bored.why: The slowness of the salons and the Albertine volumes is partly built to make the reader feel the tedium the narrator feels.

distracted.why: The digressions pull the reader sideways on purpose.

impatient.why: The reader waits with the narrator for letters and returns, and for the book to reach its end.

curious.why: The reader wants to know Odette's past, Albertine's secret, Charlus's nature, and whether the narrator will write.

surprised.why: Charlus's inversion, Saint-Loup's, Odette as the lady in pink, and the aged faces at the matinée are built to astonish.

awe.why: The final vision of time and the steeples of Martinville are built to produce wonder.

skeptical-doubtful.why: The reader is made to doubt Albertine with the narrator and to doubt the narrator's own fairness.

feeling-of-knowing.why: The madeleine scene is built so the reader strains with the narrator for the memory, and recognizes returning characters across volumes.

confused.why: The opening's disorientation and the long sentences are built to leave the reader, like the narrator, unsure where he is.

frustrated.why: The Albertine volumes are built to make the reader feel the frustration of a truth never reached.

uncertain-certain.why: The reader is kept uncertain whether Albertine loved women and whether the narrator will write, until the end.

understanding.why: Time Regained is built to give the reader the understanding of memory and art the whole novel has prepared.

inspired.why: The theory of involuntary memory and of art as recovered time is built to inspire the reader with its insight.

satisfied.why: The narrator's discovery of his vocation closes the circle, a satisfaction the reader earns.

foreboding.why: The narrator's hindsight, telling the reader what he did not know then, builds dread over Albertine and the grandmother.

nostalgia.why: The whole novel is built to make the reader feel nostalgia for a Combray and a Balbec never visited.

anticipation-suspense.why: The reader waits for secrets to surface and for the vocation to arrive, but the book is built for reverie more than suspense.

hope.why: The reader hopes the narrator will write, a hope the last volume fulfills.

schadenfreude.why: Charlus's humiliation and Legrandin's exposure are built to be enjoyed, a little.

elevation.why: The grandmother's goodness and Saint-Loup's heroism lift the reader.

infatuation.why: Swann's and the narrator's infatuations are built to be felt from within.

rage.why: Charlus's rages are observed, not shared.
